title: One Zero of f' Is Not Zero Everywhere
quickIdea: Rolle produces a point where f' = 0. That does not make f' zero everywhere: if f is not constant on the interval, f' takes a nonzero value somewhere.
remember: If f'(x) = 0 for all x in (a, b) then f is constant there, by the mean value theorem applied between any two points.
Contrapositive, which is what GATE asks: if f is not constant on the interval, then f' != 0 at some point of it.
To show f is not constant, exhibit two points with different values; one interior value is usually enough.
A function defined by a determinant is continuous and differentiable wherever its entries are, so check that no entry blows up on the interval - tan is undefined at pi/2.
Two rows of a determinant becoming equal is the standard way an endpoint value collapses to 0 without any computation.

example.prompt: GATE CSE 2014 Set 1 Q.6: f(theta) is the 3x3 determinant with first row (sin, cos, tan) at theta and the other two rows at pi/6 and pi/3. Show that both 'some theta has f'(theta) = 0' and 'some theta has f'(theta) != 0' are true on (pi/6, pi/3).
example.work: At theta = pi/6 the first two rows are identical, so f(pi/6) = 0; at theta = pi/3 the first and third rows are identical, so f(pi/3) = 0. The entries are sin, cos and tan, all differentiable on [pi/6, pi/3] because pi/2 is outside it, so Rolle gives a theta with f'(theta) = 0. At theta = pi/4 the three rows are not proportional and the determinant is 0.0977, not 0, so f is not constant and f' cannot vanish everywhere.
example.answer: Both statements hold, so the answer is option C: both I and II.

gateAngle: This is the one verified CSE question in the topic that is not a plain bound, and its second statement is the part students lose: Rolle proves existence of a zero, and the non-constant observation proves f' is not identically zero. GATE has used 'must be true' statement pairs of this kind repeatedly.

variations.label: VERIFIED PYQ
variations.question: GATE CSE 2014 Set 1 Q.6, statements I and II as above.
variations.why: I is Rolle; II is the corollary that a non-constant differentiable function cannot have f' = 0 everywhere.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: f(x) = sin x on [0, 2 pi]. Rolle gives a point with f' = 0. Is f'(x) = 0 at every point of the interval?
variations.why: The same two-step reasoning as the PYQ: existence from Rolle, non-constancy from one value. The variation isolates the step that the 2014 question rewards.

trap.what: Concluding from Rolle that f' is identically zero on the interval.
trap.why: Rolle gives one point, not an interval, and a single zero says nothing about the rest of the domain.
trap.counterexample: f(x) = x^2 - 1 on [-1, 1] has f(-1) = f(1) = 0 and f'(0) = 0, yet f'(1) = 2. The derivative is zero at exactly one point of the interval.

check.question: A differentiable f on [0, 1] satisfies f(0) = f(1) = 0 and f'(x) = 0 for all x in (0, 1). What is f?
check.explanation: Zero derivative on an interval forces a constant by the mean value theorem, and the constant is fixed by f(0) = 0.
